hook.text: A thousand requests arrive in the same second. Each one spends most of its time waiting: on a database, on another service. Serve them one after another, and the server sits idle through every wait while the queue grows.

hook-share.text: Serve them at once, and they start sharing things: a counter, a lock, a connection. That's where the bugs live.

plan.text: Sixteen questions on concurrency. Nine get a figure each, and seven go quickly at the end.

conc.text: Question one. Concurrency versus parallelism, what is the difference? Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once. One core switches between them, and each makes progress in turns.

par.text: Parallelism is doing many at the same instant, which takes more than one core.

conc-both.text: So async code on one thread is concurrent, but not parallel. Processes spread across cores are both.

conc-amdahl.text: The follow-up is what parallelism can buy. If five percent of the work can't be split, no number of cores makes it more than twenty times faster, and a hundred cores already get about seventeen. That's Amdahl's law.

proc.text: Question two. Processes versus threads, how do they differ? Threads live inside one process and share its memory, so talking is cheap: one thread writes a value, another reads it.

proc-risk.text: That sharing is also the danger. Two threads can corrupt the same state.

proc-iso.text: A crash in one can't corrupt another. In CPython, they're also how Python runs in parallel, since its threads take turns. The price is talking: data between them is usually serialized, through pipes or queues, and every process costs more memory.

race.text: Question three. What is a race condition? It's when the result depends on the timing of operations on shared state. The classic case is a counter that two threads each add one to.

race-steps.text: Adding one isn't one step. It's three: read the value, add one, write it back.

race-lost.text: The counter is at five. Both threads read five, both add one, both write six. Two increments, and one is lost.

race-count.text: Count every order those six steps can run in, and there are twenty. Only two of them give seven. The other eighteen lose an update.

race-lock.text: The fix is a lock around the three steps, so they run as one critical section. Then two orders are left, one thread first or the other, and both give seven.

race-hides.text: And since the bad orders depend on where a thread happens to pause, the same test can pass today and fail tomorrow, with no change to the code.

gil.text: Question four. What is the GIL, and why does it exist? In CPython, the standard Python interpreter, the global interpreter lock, or GIL, is a single lock that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time.
gil.spoken: Question four. What is the gill, and why does it exist? In CPython, the standard Python interpreter, the global interpreter lock, or gill, is a single lock that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time.

gil-why.text: It exists to keep memory management thread-safe. Every object counts its references, and one lock around the interpreter protects all those counts without a lock on every object.

gil-cost.text: The consequence: threads give no speedup to CPU-bound Python. They just take turns. They still help IO-bound work, because a thread releases the GIL while it waits on the network or the disk.
gil-cost.spoken: The consequence: threads give no speedup to CPU-bound Python. They just take turns. They still help IO-bound work, because a thread releases the gill while it waits on the network or the disk.

gil-race.text: And it doesn't make the counter safe. The GIL runs one bytecode instruction at a time, and that one line of Python compiles to four: load the counter, load the one, add, store. Nothing promises the four run together, so the lock is still needed.
gil-race.spoken: And it doesn't make the counter safe. The gill runs one bytecode instruction at a time, and that one line of Python compiles to four: load the counter, load the one, add, store. Nothing promises the four run together, so the lock is still needed.

gil-proc.text: For CPU-bound work, use processes instead. Each has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so they really do run in parallel.
gil-proc.spoken: For CPU-bound work, use processes instead. Each has its own interpreter and its own gill, so they really do run in parallel.

dead.text: Question five. What is a deadlock, and what four conditions cause it? A deadlock is a set of threads, each waiting forever for something another one holds.

dead-ex.text: Two threads, two locks. The first takes A, then wants B. The second takes B, then wants A. If both take their first lock before either takes its second, each waits on the other, for good.

dead-four.text: Coffman's four conditions all have to hold. Mutual exclusion: a lock has one holder at a time. Hold and wait: a thread keeps one lock while it waits for another. No preemption: nothing can take a lock away. And circular wait: a cycle of threads, each waiting on the next.

dead-break.text: Break any one, and the deadlock can't happen.

prevent.text: Question six. How do you prevent deadlocks in practice? Go after the conditions, one at a time.

prevent-order.text: Circular wait is the usual target: every thread takes its locks in one global order, A before B. Now whichever thread gets A also gets B, and the other waits holding nothing. No schedule deadlocks.

prevent-timeout.text: No preemption: take a lock with a timeout, so a thread that can't get its second lock gives up, releases its first, and tries again.

prevent-hold.text: Hold and wait: one coarse lock instead of several, so no thread holds one while it waits for another.

prevent-share.text: Mutual exclusion: share nothing. Give the state one owner thread and send it work through a queue, so no other thread needs a lock on it.

prevent-short.text: And keep critical sections short, so contention stays low.

prevent-live.text: One catch: threads that time out and retry in lockstep can collide forever. That's livelock, in the quick round.

async.text: Question seven. What is async await, and how does the event loop work? It's cooperative concurrency on a single thread. Coroutines run on an event loop. When one awaits a network call, it hands control back, and the loop runs another that's ready.

async-run.text: Two fetches: a waits twenty milliseconds, b waits ten. The waits overlap, so b finishes first, and the pair takes about twenty, not thirty. Gathered together, the results still come back in the order you asked: a, then b.

async-coop.text: The loop can only switch at an await, so a coroutine that never awaits, like a tight CPU loop, starves every other one.

async-scale.text: Where it shines is IO at high concurrency: thousands of sockets, on one thread.

block.text: Question eight. Why can't you just call a blocking function inside a coroutine? Because the loop is one thread, and a blocking call never yields.

block-run.text: Swap a's await for a blocking sleep. Now a holds the thread for its whole twenty milliseconds, and b can't even start its wait. This time a finishes first, and the pair takes thirty: the waits add up instead of overlapping.

block-server.text: In a server, that one call stalls every request on the loop until it returns. A synchronous HTTP request or a heavy computation does the same.

block-fix.text: Use async-native libraries, or hand the blocking work to a thread or process pool, and await its result.

choose.text: Question nine. When do you choose threads versus multiprocessing versus async? Match the tool to the bottleneck. The deciding question is always: is the program waiting on IO, or burning CPU?

choose-async.text: Waiting, on many connections: async. One thread, the lowest overhead.

choose-threads.text: Waiting, but through blocking libraries: threads, which release the GIL while they wait, in a pool that caps how many run.
choose-threads.spoken: Waiting, but through blocking libraries: threads, which release the gill while they wait, in a pool that caps how many run.

choose-proc.text: Burning CPU: multiprocessing. Separate processes sidestep the GIL for true parallelism.
choose-proc.spoken: Burning CPU: multiprocessing. Separate processes sidestep the gill for true parallelism.

choose-mix.text: And real services mix them: an async server that hands its heavy computation to a process pool.

rapid-in.text: Seven more, a sentence or two each.

r-lock.text: Locks, mutexes and semaphores. A mutex allows exactly one holder. A semaphore allows up to some number, say five downloads at once. And a reentrant lock can be taken again by the thread that already holds it, so recursive code doesn't deadlock on itself.

r-atomic.text: An atomic operation completes in one indivisible step: no other thread can see it half done. Adding one to the counter isn't atomic.

r-safe.text: Thread-safe code behaves correctly when many threads call it at once. Avoid shared mutable state, guard it with a lock, or best, keep it in one thread and send that thread work through a thread-safe queue. Share by communicating, not by sharing memory.

r-live.text: In a livelock, threads keep running but make no progress: they react to each other and retry, like two people stepping aside the same way, again and again. The CPU looks busy, so it's harder to spot than a deadlock. Randomized backoff usually breaks it.

r-starve.text: Starvation is a thread that never gets the resource, because others keep getting priority, like a low-priority thread that never wins a lock. Fair locks help, and so does not handing out shared resources by priority.

r-pool.text: A thread pool keeps a fixed set of reusable workers and a queue of tasks. You skip creating a thread per task, and you bound how many run at once.

r-future.text: And a future is a claim ticket for a result that isn't ready yet. Start the work, take the ticket at once, and collect the value later, by blocking on it or awaiting it.

next.text: All of this was about code running at the same time.

next-change.text: Just as hard is code that has to keep changing without breaking. Next: designing objects.

gil-free.text: Since Python three fourteen, there's also an officially supported build with no GIL. There, threads do run in parallel, so the counter's lock matters even more.
gil-free.spoken: Since Python three fourteen, there's also an officially supported build with no gill. There, threads do run in parallel, so the counter's lock matters even more.

prevent-all.text: Or take every lock you need at once.

prevent-detect.text: If one happens anyway, a thread dump shows who's waiting on whom.

async-os.text: Under it, the loop asks the operating system which sockets are ready, and wakes the coroutines waiting on them.

r-cas.text: An atomic add instruction makes it so, or compare-and-swap: write only if the value is unchanged since the read, and retry if not. Or hold a lock around all three.

r-promise.text: A promise is the same idea, seen from the side that fills in the value.

proc-own.text: Processes each get their own memory.
